analysis.one_liner: Caps payday loan fees and rollovers, but overrides state laws that cap or ban payday lending.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or vote, dying when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cap what payday lenders can charge at 15 cents per dollar borrowed, limit loan refinancing to two consecutive times, and give every borrower the right once a year to convert a loan into a four-payment plan at no charge, with no collections during that plan. It would also require signed written loan agreements, posted warnings, and surety bonds from lenders. But the same bill would preempt — override — state laws that cap rates, restrict refinancing, or ban payday lending altogether for loans charging more than 36% annual interest, replacing those stricter state rules with a single national standard set at roughly what payday lenders already charge.
analysis.who_benefits: Payday borrowers get real protections against debt spirals: refinancing capped at two times, a lower fee on each refinancing, one free extended payment plan per year, clearer disclosures in their own language, and a bonded lender with money on the line. Payday lenders also gain: a federal framework that makes their product legal nationwide and frees them from stricter state rate caps and state bans.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total interest and fees at 15 cents per dollar on an original payday loan, drops the cap to 10 cents per dollar on a second refinancing, and bans origination fees on refinanced loans.
Prohibits refinancing a payday loan more than two consecutive times and requires each refinancing to be a new agreement signed by both the lender and the borrower.

Gives borrowers who cannot repay the right, once in any 12-month period, to opt into a free extended payment plan splitting the balance into four equal payments, and bars any collection activity during that plan.

Requires a signed written loan agreement stating the total dollar cost of the loan, in English and in the language the loan was negotiated, plus conspicuous warnings that the loan is not for long-term needs and that the borrower cannot be criminally prosecuted for it.

Requires payday lenders to file a surety bond — $100,000 per store, or $1 million for lenders with 10 or more stores or online lending — for the benefit of the state attorney general, so there is money available if the lender breaks the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers in states that went further than this bill — states with 36% rate caps, bans, or tighter refinancing rules — would lose those stronger protections, because the bill preempts state laws limiting rates and fees for loans charging more than 36% annual interest.
analysis.who_pays_short: Borrowers in states with stricter laws

drawbacks.text: The preemption clause overrides state laws that limit rates and fees, restrict refinancing, or mandate or restrict payment plans for any payday loan charging more than 36% annual interest, so a state with a 36% cap or an outright payday lending ban could not enforce it against a lender following this federal standard.

The 15-cents-per-dollar cap is set at roughly standard payday pricing: on a typical two-week loan, 15% works out to about a 390% annual percentage rate, so the cap ratifies what lenders already charge rather than lowering it.

Charges for default, delinquency, or a bounced payment — up to the greater of $25 or the bank's own charge — are excluded from the fee cap entirely, leaving room for additional costs on top of the 15%.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill honestly targets the worst harm of payday lending — serial rollovers that trap borrowers — with a two-refinancing limit, cheaper refinancings, and a free exit ramp once a year. But it pays for those protections by stripping stricter rules from states that already have them, and its headline fee cap matches the market rate rather than cutting it. A borrower in a state with a 36% cap or a lending ban would be worse off under this bill; a borrower in a permissive state would be modestly better off. It is a national floor set at the industry's standard price, traded away stronger state-level protections to get it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Baca (D-CA) introduced the bill on April 1, 2009, joined by Rep. Jean Schmidt (R-OH).
The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee the same day, and the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
It attracted 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican — before expiring at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, no federal preemption took effect, so states kept their own payday laws. Borrowers in states with strict caps or lending bans are the clearest winners; the payday industry gained nothing but also lost nothing, since the modest new protections never arrived either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Borrowers in states with strict payday laws

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican cosponsored — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how support would have split.

industries.note: The bill would lock payday lending into federal law nationwide, capping fees at 15% per loan term — about the industry's standard price — and preempting stricter state rate caps and bans for loans above 36% APR. Lenders would give up unlimited rollovers and gain legal certainty across every state; borrowers in tough-on-payday states would lose their stronger protections. For borrowers in permissive states, the bill's rollover limits and free extended payment plan run alongside their interest, which is why the stance is not purely one-sided.
Collection activity would be barred during a borrower's extended payment plan, removing one pressure tactic during the plan period.
A new bonding requirement for every payday lender would create a market for surety bonds filed for the benefit of state attorneys general.
